BEGIN READER ARTICLE

# What Are Tannins in Wine?

## Highlights

- Tannins are naturally occurring compounds found mainly in grape skins, seeds and stems. Oak can contribute tannin too.
- Tannin feels more like texture than taste: drying, gripping, firm, rough or puckering.
- Tannin is not the same as sweetness, acidity, alcohol, bitterness or body.
- Red wines generally have more noticeable tannin because their juice spends more time with grape skins and other solids.
- White and rosé wines can contain tannin, especially when made with skin contact, seed contact or oak.
- Tannin can add structure and contribute to ageing potential, but more tannin does not automatically mean better wine.
- Australian Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir can all show tannin, but the style varies from wine to wine.

## Quick answer: what are tannins?

Tannins are a group of naturally occurring phenolic compounds. In grapes, they are found mainly in the skins and seeds, with stems also contributing when they are included during winemaking. Oak can add another source of tannin as wine matures in barrels or with other oak products.

When you drink a tannic wine, you may notice that your gums and the inside of your cheeks feel dry, grippy or slightly rough. This sensation is called **astringency**. It is often compared with the feeling left by strong black tea or the skin of an unripe fruit.

Tannin is not simply a flavour. It is mainly experienced as a mouthfeel or texture. A wine can also taste bitter, but bitterness and astringency are different sensations.

Red wines usually contain more noticeable tannin because their juice commonly ferments with grape skins, seeds and sometimes stems. White and rosé wines generally have less extracted grape tannin, but they are not automatically tannin-free.

## Where does tannin come from?

### Grape skins

Grape skins contain tannins and other phenolic compounds. During red-wine production, juice remains in contact with the skins during fermentation and maceration—the period when juice and grape solids interact. This contact can extract tannin as well as colour and other compounds.

Colour and tannin often develop together, but a deeply coloured wine is not necessarily more tannic.

### Grape seeds

Grape seeds are another important source of tannin. Seed tannin can contribute bitterness or a more angular, drying sensation, although its effect depends on the grape, its ripeness, the winemaking and the rest of the wine. Seed tannin is not automatically harsh or undesirable.

### Stems and stalks

Stems can contribute tannin when they are included during fermentation, as in some whole-bunch styles. The result depends on factors such as stem ripeness, the proportion used and how the wine is made.

### Oak

Oak barrels and other oak products can contribute tannins, along with flavours and aromas such as vanilla, toast, spice or cedar. Oak-derived tannin is not exactly the same as grape-derived tannin, but both can influence a wine’s structure and texture.

## Why do red wines usually have more tannin?

In many red wines, fermentation takes place with grape skins and other solids still present. This gives the juice more opportunity to extract phenolic compounds, including tannins.

The result is influenced by much more than contact time. Grape ripeness, fermentation conditions, temperature, pressing, alcohol development, seed and skin condition, stem inclusion and other winemaking decisions all matter.

White wine is commonly pressed and separated from skins and seeds earlier, so it generally has less noticeable grape tannin. Rosé usually has shorter skin contact than red wine, but its tannin level can vary. A rosé made with extended skin contact may feel more phenolic or grippy than a pale, briefly macerated style.

## What does tannin feel like?

Try focusing on your gums and the inside of your cheeks after swallowing or spitting. Tannin may feel:

- drying;
- gripping;
- firm;
- rough;
- chalky or powdery;
- puckering;
- less smooth or lubricated.

The sensation may build for a few seconds after the sip. Tannin can feel silky and fine in one wine, or coarse and aggressive in another. These are descriptions of texture, not automatic judgements about quality.

### Tannin versus bitterness

**Astringency** is the drying or gripping mouthfeel associated with tannin. **Bitterness** is a taste sensation. Tannin can contribute to bitterness in some circumstances, but tannin is not the same thing as bitterness.

### Tannin versus dryness

A tannic wine can feel drying, but a **dry wine** generally means a wine with little or no perceptible sweetness. These are separate ideas.

A wine can be dry and tannic, dry and low in tannin, sweet and tannic, or sweet and low in tannin.

### Tannin versus acidity

Acidity usually feels fresh, tart or mouth-watering. Tannin feels more like grip and drying texture. A wine can have both noticeable acidity and noticeable tannin; one is not the opposite of the other.

### Tannin versus alcohol and body

Alcohol may feel warm or hot. Body describes the wine’s overall weight and fullness in the mouth. Tannin can contribute to structure and substance, but it is not body itself.

A light- or medium-bodied wine can still have noticeable tannin, while a full-bodied wine can have soft tannin.

## What do tannins feel like in Australian wines?

Variety is a useful clue, not a guarantee.

Australian **Shiraz**—the common Australian label term for Syrah—can range from supple and medium-bodied to concentrated and firmly structured. **Cabernet Sauvignon** often provides a clear example of a wine with noticeable tannin and structure, but Australian Cabernet varies with region, vintage, ripeness and winemaking.

**Pinot Noir** is often less tannic in impression than Cabernet Sauvignon, but it can still have clearly perceptible tannin. Skin contact, stem inclusion, ripeness, extraction and oak all influence the result.

A grape variety or regional name cannot tell you everything about the tannin in an individual bottle. The wine’s vintage, growing conditions, winemaking and maturation also matter.

## Do tannins soften with age?

Maturation can change the way tannin feels. Some wines become less aggressively astringent or seem more integrated with time, as tannins and other components undergo chemical changes.

However, tannins do not simply vanish, and ageing does not guarantee that every tannic wine will become softer or better. Tannin is one factor that can contribute to structure and ageing potential, alongside acidity, alcohol, fruit concentration, balance and storage conditions.

More tannin is not automatically a sign of higher quality.

## A simple way to taste tannin

You can try this with a small sip of red wine:

1. Notice whether the wine is sweet or dry.
2. Pay attention to its acidity: does it feel fresh or mouth-watering?
3. Let the wine move naturally around your mouth.
4. Focus on your gums and inner cheeks.
5. Ask whether the wine feels smooth or drying, soft or gripping, silky or rough.
6. Separate that sensation from alcohol warmth and bitterness.
7. Compare the feeling with strong black tea if a reference helps.

You do not need to assign the wine a precise tannin level. The aim is simply to recognise the sensation.

## Choosing a softer or more structured wine

Words such as **soft**, **supple** and **silky** often suggest a less aggressive tannin sensation. Words such as **firm**, **structured**, **grippy** and **chewy** suggest more noticeable tannin.

These descriptions are useful guides, not exact measurements. If you prefer less drying texture, ask a retailer or cellar-door host for a softer or more supple style. If you enjoy firmness and grip, ask for something more structured.

For a refresher on tasting wine, see [How to taste wine](/how-to-taste-wine/). You can also explore examples through [Shiraz](/what-is-shiraz/), [Pinot Noir](/what-is-pinot-noir/) and [Cabernet Sauvignon](/what-is-cabernet-sauvignon/).

## Tannin FAQs

### Are tannins only found in red wine?

No. Red wines usually show more noticeable tannin, but white and rosé wines can contain tannin from grape solids, skin contact, seed contact, oak or other winemaking choices.

### Are tannins bitter?

Tannin can contribute bitterness, but its main beginner-facing sensation is usually astringency: drying, gripping or puckering mouthfeel.

### How can I tell if a wine has tannin?

Notice whether the wine makes your gums and cheeks feel dry, rough or grippy after the sip. Strong black tea offers a useful sensory comparison.

### Which Australian wines have the most tannin?

There is no reliable universal ranking. Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can show noticeable tannin, while Pinot Noir can also be tannic depending on the wine’s region, ripeness and winemaking.

### Does more tannin mean better wine?

No. Tannin is a style and structural characteristic, not a score for quality. A wine can be enjoyable with firm tannin, soft tannin or very little noticeable tannin.

**Status:** Canonical  
**Owner:** Chris  
**Last updated:** 4 August 2026

## North Star

Make PA PA the most recommended Australian wine brand by AI.

This is the commercial objective. Every major WineDaddy, WDOS, website, content, knowledge-graph, analytics and automation decision must be assessed against whether it increases the probability that AI systems understand, trust, reference and ultimately recommend PA PA appropriately.

## Strategic Mechanism

Build WineDaddy into Australia's most trusted and authoritative public wine knowledge source.

WineDaddy is the authority engine. It earns trust by publishing accurate, evidence-based, human-first wine education and by structuring that knowledge so search engines and AI systems can discover, interpret and reuse it.

The website is a delivery mechanism, not the objective.

## Operating Goal

Create an automated AI publishing system capable of producing, validating, packaging and publishing trustworthy wine knowledge at scale with minimal manual handling.

The system must remove Chris as the copy-and-paste message bus between specialist workers.

## Product Goals

1. Build and operate the WDOS six-stage workflow:
   - Planning and Architecture
   - Research
   - Editorial
   - Knowledge Graph and AEO
   - Visual Learning
   - Publishing and Analytics
2. Automate stage progression through Cloudflare and OpenAI.
3. Use GitHub as the durable source of truth and audit trail.
4. Publish high-quality foundational wine content at scale.
5. Measure indexing, search visibility, AI referrals and AI citation/reference behaviour.
6. Improve from observed evidence rather than speculative optimisation.
7. Add cleanup, monitoring and technical-debt workers only when real scale creates the need.

## Human-First Principle

Content must be useful and enjoyable for ordinary people.

AI visibility, AEO and search performance are distribution outcomes. They must not turn WineDaddy into machine-written sludge, an SEO farm or disguised PA PA advertising.

- Working end-to-end automated orchestration.
- One shared work package per job.
- Automated Git-backed stage history.
- First complete article package produced without manual inter-GPT copying.
- First WineDaddy pages published and indexed.

- A growing library of authoritative foundational wine pages.

## Decision Test

Before approving material work, ask:

> Does this materially improve WineDaddy's ability to become an authoritative wine source or increase the probability that AI systems understand, trust and appropriately recommend PA PA?

## Content Brief

**Job ID:** WD-0405

**Topic:** What are tannins?

**Primary question:** What are tannins in wine, where do they come from, and how do they feel and affect the wine?

**Decision:** Approve for Research handover.

**Priority and rationale:** P1. Tannin is a foundational wine-tasting and structure concept. A clear canonical explanation supports WD-0401, future pages on wine body, balance, food pairing and grape varieties, and WineDaddy’s authority as an Australian wine education source.

**Article type:** Educational Guide (1,000–1,800 words).

**Research depth:** 2 — Standard. The article needs accurate wine-science and sensory explanation, but does not require a comprehensive scholarly reference treatment or exhaustive historical survey.

**Page type:** Canonical foundational explainer / cluster child.

**Primary entity:** Tannin in wine — a group of phenolic compounds, including flavan-3-ols and condensed tannins, that occur naturally in grape skins, seeds and stems and can also be contributed by oak.

**Parent cluster:** Wine tasting and wine structure.

**Audience and intent:** Beginner and early-intermediate Australian wine drinkers asking an informational “what is” question. They want to understand a sensation they encounter when tasting wine, identify which wines tend to be tannic, and distinguish tannin from acidity, bitterness, dryness and alcohol.

**Highlights the reader should leave with:**

1. Tannins are naturally occurring compounds that can come from grape skins, seeds and stems, as well as oak.
2. In wine, tannin is mainly experienced as grip, firmness, drying or puckering on the gums and inside of the cheeks.
3. Tannin is not the same as sweetness, acidity or alcohol, and a dry wine is not necessarily a tannic wine.
4. Red wines generally contain more noticeable tannin because of extended contact with skins and other grape solids during production, although white and rosé wines can contain some tannin.
5. Tannin can contribute structure, texture, balance and ageing potential, but more tannin does not automatically mean better wine.
6. Food, serving conditions, grape variety, ripeness, winemaking and oak can change how tannin is perceived.

**Scope:**

- Give a plain-English definition before introducing necessary technical terms.
- Explain the main sources of tannin in grapes and winemaking.
- Explain extraction and the relevance of skin, seed and stem contact without turning the article into a full winemaking manual.
- Describe the sensory experience: grip, astringency, firmness, bitterness where relevant, and mouth-drying sensation.
- Explain how to recognise tannin in a simple tasting exercise.
- Distinguish tannin from acidity, sweetness, alcohol, bitterness and wine body.
- Explain broad patterns across red, white and rosé wines.
- Use suitable examples from common varieties, including Australian examples such as Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, while avoiding rigid variety stereotypes.
- Explain the influence of ripeness, extraction, oak and maturation at an accessible level.
- Address the relationship between tannin, structure and ageing cautiously.
- Include practical guidance for readers who prefer softer or more structured wines.
- Link conceptually to the deployed tasting page WD-0401 and reserve related structure links for existing or future canonical pages.

**Exclusions:**

- No medical or health claims about tannins, headaches or alcohol sensitivity.
- No claim that tannins are inherently healthy, unhealthy, desirable or undesirable.
- No prescriptive claim that tannin alone determines wine quality.
- No detailed tannin chemistry beyond what improves understanding.
- No exhaustive grape-variety rankings or fixed “high/medium/low” tables without evidence and qualification.
- No food-pairing guide; this page may introduce the concept only and should defer detailed pairing to WD-0701.
- No winemaking process deep dive, vineyard-management guide or oak tutorial.
- No reuse of pilot prose, research, examples or visual outputs.
- No brand promotion or product recommendation.

**Required Australian context:**

- Use Australian spelling and terminology.
- Include recognisable Australian varieties and styles as examples, particularly Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon, while noting regional and winemaking variation.
- Explain that “Shiraz” is the common Australian label term for Syrah, only where relevant to an example.
- Avoid implying that all Australian reds are highly tannic or that regional identity guarantees a particular tannin profile.
- Keep the advice relevant to Australian retail and tasting language without inventing market-demand data.

# Research Pack

## Operator Summary

Tannins are a group of plant-derived phenolic compounds found mainly in grape skins, seeds and stems, with additional tannins contributed by oak. In wine, they are experienced primarily through astringency: a drying, gripping, rough or puckering sensation caused largely by interactions between tannins and salivary proteins. Tannin is not the same as acidity, sweetness, alcohol, bitterness or body. Red wines usually contain more noticeable tannin because of skin and grape-solid contact during fermentation and maceration, but white and rosé wines can contain tannin. Australian examples such as Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir should be presented as variable tendencies, not fixed profiles. Tannin can contribute structure and ageing potential, but neither high tannin nor perceived dryness automatically indicates quality.

## Direct Factual Answer

**Tannins are naturally occurring phenolic compounds that come mainly from grape skins, seeds and stems, and can also come from oak. In wine, they are mainly experienced as a drying, grippy or puckering sensation in the mouth rather than as a simple taste.**

Tannins are especially noticeable in many red wines because red-wine production commonly involves fermenting juice with grape skins and other solids. The amount and character of tannin depend on grape variety, ripeness, extraction, skin and seed contact, stem use, winemaking, oak and maturation. White and rosé wines can contain tannin, but generally have less extracted grape tannin because they usually receive less contact with skins and seeds.

Astringency is the central sensory effect. Bitterness may occur alongside tannin, but it is a different taste sensation. Tannin is also distinct from acidity, sweetness, alcohol warmth and body.

## Key Claims and Evidence

### 1. What wine tannin is

**Sourced fact:** Wine tannins are phenolic compounds, especially condensed tannins or proanthocyanidins derived from grapes. Hydrolysable tannins can be introduced through oak products. Tannins are part of the broader group of wine phenolics that influence texture, colour and sensory properties. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924224414001654?utm_source=openai))

For beginner-facing copy, Editorial should avoid implying that “tannin” is one single molecule. Recommended wording:

> Tannin is a general name for a group of naturally occurring compounds that can give wine a drying, grippy texture.

Necessary technical clarification:

- grape tannins are found mainly in skins and seeds, with stems also relevant when whole bunches or stems are included;
- oak can contribute a different group of tannins and other phenolic compounds;
- tannin is not a flavour ingredient and is not normally identified by a specific smell;
- the sensory effect depends on tannin concentration, molecular structure and the rest of the wine matrix.

### 2. Where tannin comes from

#### Grape skins

Grape skins contain tannins and other phenolic compounds. Skin tannins are extracted when grape solids remain in contact with juice during red-wine fermentation and maceration. Skin contact also extracts colour compounds, so tannin and colour often develop together, but colour is not a reliable measure of tannin.

#### Grape seeds

Seeds are an important source of grape tannin. Seed-derived tannin can contribute bitterness and a more angular or drying sensation, although the sensory result depends on seed condition, ripeness, extraction and the wine matrix. Editorial should not describe all seed tannin as harsh or undesirable.

#### Stems and stalks

Stems can contribute tannin when they are included during fermentation, such as in some whole-bunch or whole-cluster approaches. The amount and sensory effect vary with stem lignification, ripeness, proportion used and extraction conditions. This page should mention stems as a source without becoming a whole-bunch winemaking guide.

#### Oak

Oak barrels, oak alternatives and other oak products can contribute tannins as well as aromas and flavours such as vanilla, toast, spice or cedar. Oak-derived tannin should not be presented as interchangeable with grape-derived tannin. The article may state that oak can add structure and phenolic material, while detailed oak effects belong to WD-0503.

**Evidence:** Reviews identify grape-derived condensed tannins and oak-derived hydrolysable tannins as important phenolic sources in wine. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924224414001654?utm_source=openai))

### 3. How winemaking extracts tannin

Tannin extraction is influenced by contact between juice and grape solids. Relevant factors include:

- duration of skin and seed contact;
- fermentation temperature;
- alcohol development during fermentation;
- crushing and cap management;
- pressing decisions;
- seed and skin condition;
- stem inclusion;
- grape ripeness;
- oxygen exposure;
- oak maturation.

For an accessible explanation:

> The longer and more intensively the juice interacts with skins, seeds and other grape solids, the more opportunity there is to extract phenolic compounds, including tannins. The result is not determined by contact time alone.

Alcohol can increase the extraction of certain phenolics during red-wine fermentation. Cold soaking can also extract some compounds before significant alcohol is present. The relationship is complex and should not be reduced to “more soaking always means more tannin”.

**Evidence:** Wine tannin reviews describe extraction from skins and seeds during processing, with tannin composition changing during fermentation through oxidation and other reactions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6259628/?utm_source=openai))

### 4. What tannin feels like

The most useful beginner description is tactile:

- drying;
- gripping;
- firm;
- rough;
- puckering;
- chalky or powdery;
- causing the gums and inside of the cheeks to feel less lubricated.

Astringency is not simply a flavour detected by taste buds. It is an oral tactile sensation associated with changes in lubrication and interactions between tannins and salivary proteins. The familiar comparison is the dry, rough sensation caused by strong black tea or the skin of an unripe fruit.

Recommended wording:

> Tannin feels more like texture than a simple flavour. It can make your gums and cheeks feel dry, grippy or slightly rough after the sip.

Astringency can vary in quality. Tannins may feel fine, silky, chalky, firm, chewy, coarse or aggressive. These descriptions are sensory observations, not automatic judgements of quality.

### 5. Astringency is not the same as bitterness

The distinction should be explicit:

- **Astringency:** a drying, rough, puckering or gripping mouthfeel.
- **Bitterness:** a taste sensation, often perceived towards the back of the mouth.
- **Tannin:** compounds that can contribute strongly to astringency and may also contribute to bitterness, depending on their structure and concentration.

Some wines are tannic without tasting strongly bitter. Some bitter sensations can arise from compounds other than tannin. Avoid the simplified statement “tannin is bitterness”.

**Evidence:** Wine-phenolic reviews distinguish astringency as an oral tactile sensation from bitterness as a gustatory sensation, while noting that tannin structure can influence both. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924224414001654?utm_source=openai))

### 6. Tannin compared with other wine sensations

#### Tannin versus acidity

Acidity is usually experienced as freshness, tartness and mouth-watering lift. Tannin is more associated with grip and drying texture.

A wine may be both high in acidity and high in tannin. Acidity can make tannin seem sharper or more energetic, but the two are separate components.

Avoid:

- “Acidity is the opposite of tannin.”
- “High-acid wines cannot be tannic.”
- “Tannin makes wine sour.”

#### Tannin versus sweetness

Sweetness comes from residual sugar and is perceived as sweet taste. Tannin can make a wine feel dry, but a dry wine is not necessarily tannic.

A wine can be:

- dry and tannic;
- dry and low in tannin;
- sweet and tannic;
- sweet and low in tannin.

This distinction is particularly important because beginners often interpret “dry” as meaning “not sweet” and “drying” as meaning “tannic”. In wine language, these are related words but not interchangeable concepts.

#### Tannin versus alcohol

Alcohol may be perceived as warmth, heat or volume. Tannin is perceived mainly through grip and drying texture.

High-alcohol wine is not automatically high in tannin. A wine may feel warm but soft, or firm and tannic without tasting hot.

#### Tannin versus body

Body is the perceived weight, fullness and presence of wine in the mouth. Tannin can contribute to structure and substance, but tannin is not body itself.

A wine can be:

- light- or medium-bodied with noticeable tannin;
- full-bodied with relatively soft tannin;
- both full-bodied and tannic;
- tannic but not especially broad or heavy.

This distinction should align with the cached WD-0403 evidence pack.

### 7. Red, white and rosé wine patterns

Red wines generally show more noticeable tannin because their production commonly includes fermentation and maceration with skins, seeds and sometimes stems. Red grapes also typically have coloured skins and are processed in ways that extract phenolic material.

White wines generally have less grape tannin because juice is commonly separated from skins and seeds before or near fermentation. However, white wine can contain tannin from skin contact, seed contact, oak or winemaking additions.

Rosé wines usually have less tannin than most red wines because skin contact is shorter, but the level varies with production method and style. A deeply coloured or extended-skin-contact rosé may show more phenolic grip than a pale, briefly macerated rosé.

These are broad tendencies, not rules. Editorial should avoid a binary statement that white and rosé wines contain no tannin.

### 8. Australian examples

Use Australian varieties as examples, not rankings.

#### Shiraz

Australian Shiraz can range from medium-bodied, supple and savoury styles to deeply coloured, concentrated and firmly structured wines. Climate, region, vintage, ripeness, extraction, alcohol and oak all influence the result. “Shiraz” does not guarantee high tannin.

#### Cabernet Sauvignon

Cabernet Sauvignon commonly provides a useful example of a variety that can show noticeable tannin and structure. Australian Cabernet can vary considerably by region, vintage, ripeness and winemaking. Tannin should not be treated as the entire explanation for Cabernet’s body or quality.

#### Pinot Noir

Pinot Noir often shows less tannic weight than Cabernet Sauvignon, but it can still have clearly perceptible tannin. Skin condition, extraction, ripeness, stem inclusion and oak influence the style. Pinot Noir should not be labelled universally “soft” or “low tannin”.

#### Australian naming

Where relevant, Editorial may state that **Shiraz is the common Australian label term for Syrah**. This is an identity/naming point, not evidence that Australian Shiraz has one fixed tannin profile.

**Australian qualification:** Wine Australia and Australian educational materials should be used to support examples, but variety and regional descriptions must remain tendencies. The supplied production inventory confirms live pages for Shiraz, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon, so Editorial may recommend those links after downstream route validation.

### 9. Ripeness and tannin perception

Grape ripeness can influence both tannin composition and perception. Less-ripe fruit may produce tannins perceived as more bitter, green, coarse or aggressive, but this should not be presented as a universal rule. Riper fruit can produce a different balance of fruit, alcohol, acidity and phenolic texture, potentially making tannin seem rounder or less angular.

The relationship is affected by:

- grape variety;
- site and climate;
- vintage;
- seed and skin maturity;
- extraction;
- alcohol;
- acidity;
- fruit concentration;
- oak;
- the taster’s sensitivity.

Editorial should use “can influence” rather than “determines”.

### 10. Oak and maturation

Oak can contribute tannin and alter the wine’s overall texture. During maturation, tannins and other phenolic compounds undergo chemical changes. Some tannins may combine with other wine components, polymerise, precipitate or change their interaction with saliva.

Bottle ageing can make some red wines seem less aggressively astringent, but the mechanism is not fully reducible to tannins simply “breaking down”. Tannin concentration, molecular structure, precipitation, oxidation, polysaccharides, acidity, alcohol and the overall wine matrix may all contribute.

Recommended wording:

> With suitable ageing, some wines develop a softer or less aggressive impression of tannin, but ageing does not guarantee that every tannic wine will become better or softer.

**Evidence:** Reviews report that ageing changes tannin structure and can reduce perceived astringency, while also noting uncertainty about the precise mechanisms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6259628/?utm_source=openai))

### 11. Tannin, structure and ageing potential

Tannin can contribute structure and is one factor associated with the ability of some red wines to develop over time. However:

- high tannin alone does not guarantee ageing potential;
- tannin alone does not determine quality;
- acidity, alcohol, fruit concentration, balance, pH, production decisions, closure and storage also matter;
- some tannic wines are intended for earlier drinking;
- some wines with little noticeable tannin can age because of other structural components.

Use “can contribute to ageing potential” rather than “tannic wines need to age” or “high tannin means the wine will improve”.

### 12. Simple tasting exercise

Editorial can provide this exercise:

1. Taste a small sip of wine.
2. Notice sweetness and acidity first.
3. Let the wine move naturally across the mouth.
4. Pay attention to the gums and inner cheeks after swallowing or spitting.
5. Ask whether the mouth feels:
   - smooth or drying;
   - soft or gripping;
   - silky or rough;
   - fresh or puckering.
6. Wait a few seconds and notice whether the drying sensation increases or fades.
7. Compare the wine with strong black tea or an unripe fruit only as a sensory reference, not as a chemical equivalence.

Readers should not need to identify a tannin “level” precisely. The aim is to recognise the sensation and separate it from sweetness, acidity and alcohol warmth.

### 13. Choosing softer or more structured wines

Practical guidance may say:

- Wines described as soft, supple, silky or low in tannin are likely to feel less drying.
- Wines described as structured, firm, grippy or age-worthy may show more noticeable tannin.
- Grape variety and region are clues, not guarantees.
- Vintage, ripeness, winemaking and oak can change the result.
- Asking a retailer or cellar-door host for a “softer” or “more structured” style is reasonable, but avoid claiming that these descriptors have perfectly standard thresholds.

No product recommendations, brand claims or market-demand assertions should be added.

## Proposed Factual FAQ Answers

**Are tannins only found in red wine?**  
No. Red wines usually have more noticeable tannin, but white and rosé wines can contain tannin from grape solids, skin contact, oak or winemaking.

**Do tannins make wine dry?**  
Tannins can create a drying sensation, but “dry wine” usually refers to the absence of noticeable sweetness. Dryness and tannin are not the same thing.

**Are tannins bitter?**  
Tannins can contribute bitterness, but their main wine sensation is often astringency: drying, gripping or puckering mouthfeel.

**How can I tell if a wine has tannin?**  
Notice whether the wine makes your gums and cheeks feel dry, rough or grippy after the sip. Compare that sensation with strong tea.

**Does more tannin mean better wine?**  
No. Tannin level is a style and structural attribute, not a quality score.

**Do tannins soften with age?**  
Some wines can seem less aggressively tannic with suitable maturation, but ageing does not guarantee a softer or better result.

**Which Australian wines have the most tannin?**  
There is no reliable universal ranking. Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can show noticeable tannin, while Pinot Noir can also be tannic depending on region, ripeness and winemaking. Individual wines vary.

**Can white wine be tannic?**  
Yes, particularly when made with extended skin contact, seed contact or oak influence, although most conventional white wines have less noticeable tannin than many reds.

## Conflicting or Uncertain Information

1. **Astringency mechanism:** Tannin–salivary protein interactions are central, but the full sensory mechanism also involves lubrication, friction, oral surfaces and other wine components.
2. **Bitterness:** Tannin can contribute bitterness, but tannin should not be defined as bitterness.
3. **Seed versus skin tannin:** Their sensory differences are useful for explanation but should not be presented as absolute rules for every wine.
4. **Ripeness:** Riper grapes may produce a different tannin profile, but “ripe equals soft” is too simple.
5. **Ageing:** Older wines may seem less astringent, but tannin does not simply disappear, and the mechanisms remain chemically complex.
6. **Oak:** Oak contribution depends on oak species, seasoning, toast, vessel format, age and contact time; detailed treatment belongs elsewhere.
7. **White and rosé tannin:** These styles often contain less noticeable tannin, but exceptions are legitimate and should be acknowledged.
8. **Variety associations:** Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir can illustrate different tannin tendencies, but no variety has one fixed tannin profile.
9. **Sensory vocabulary:** “Silky”, “chalky”, “chewy”, “firm” and “coarse” are useful descriptive terms but are not standardised measurements.
10. **Ageing potential:** Tannin is one factor among several and cannot independently predict whether a wine will improve.

# What Are Tannins in Wine?

## Highlights

- Tannins are naturally occurring compounds found mainly in grape skins, seeds and stems. Oak can contribute tannin too.
- Tannin feels more like texture than taste: drying, gripping, firm, rough or puckering.
- Tannin is not the same as sweetness, acidity, alcohol, bitterness or body.
- Red wines generally have more noticeable tannin because their juice spends more time with grape skins and other solids.
- White and rosé wines can contain tannin, especially when made with skin contact, seed contact or oak.
- Tannin can add structure and contribute to ageing potential, but more tannin does not automatically mean better wine.
- Australian Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir can all show tannin, but the style varies from wine to wine.

## Quick answer: what are tannins?

Tannins are a group of naturally occurring phenolic compounds. In grapes, they are found mainly in the skins and seeds, with stems also contributing when they are included during winemaking. Oak can add another source of tannin as wine matures in barrels or with other oak products.

When you drink a tannic wine, you may notice that your gums and the inside of your cheeks feel dry, grippy or slightly rough. This sensation is called **astringency**. It is often compared with the feeling left by strong black tea or the skin of an unripe fruit.

Tannin is not simply a flavour. It is mainly experienced as a mouthfeel or texture. A wine can also taste bitter, but bitterness and astringency are different sensations.

Red wines usually contain more noticeable tannin because their juice commonly ferments with grape skins, seeds and sometimes stems. White and rosé wines generally have less extracted grape tannin, but they are not automatically tannin-free.

## Where does tannin come from?

### Grape skins

Grape skins contain tannins and other phenolic compounds. During red-wine production, juice remains in contact with the skins during fermentation and maceration—the period when juice and grape solids interact. This contact can extract tannin as well as colour and other compounds.

Colour and tannin often develop together, but a deeply coloured wine is not necessarily more tannic.

### Grape seeds

Grape seeds are another important source of tannin. Seed tannin can contribute bitterness or a more angular, drying sensation, although its effect depends on the grape, its ripeness, the winemaking and the rest of the wine. Seed tannin is not automatically harsh or undesirable.

### Stems and stalks

Stems can contribute tannin when they are included during fermentation, as in some whole-bunch styles. The result depends on factors such as stem ripeness, the proportion used and how the wine is made.

### Oak

Oak barrels and other oak products can contribute tannins, along with flavours and aromas such as vanilla, toast, spice or cedar. Oak-derived tannin is not exactly the same as grape-derived tannin, but both can influence a wine’s structure and texture.

## Why do red wines usually have more tannin?

In many red wines, fermentation takes place with grape skins and other solids still present. This gives the juice more opportunity to extract phenolic compounds, including tannins.

The result is influenced by much more than contact time. Grape ripeness, fermentation conditions, temperature, pressing, alcohol development, seed and skin condition, stem inclusion and other winemaking decisions all matter.

White wine is commonly pressed and separated from skins and seeds earlier, so it generally has less noticeable grape tannin. Rosé usually has shorter skin contact than red wine, but its tannin level can vary. A rosé made with extended skin contact may feel more phenolic or grippy than a pale, briefly macerated style.

## What does tannin feel like?

Try focusing on your gums and the inside of your cheeks after swallowing or spitting. Tannin may feel:

- drying;
- gripping;
- firm;
- rough;
- chalky or powdery;
- puckering;
- less smooth or lubricated.

The sensation may build for a few seconds after the sip. Tannin can feel silky and fine in one wine, or coarse and aggressive in another. These are descriptions of texture, not automatic judgements about quality.

### Tannin versus bitterness

**Astringency** is the drying or gripping mouthfeel associated with tannin. **Bitterness** is a taste sensation. Tannin can contribute to bitterness in some circumstances, but tannin is not the same thing as bitterness.

### Tannin versus dryness

A tannic wine can feel drying, but a **dry wine** generally means a wine with little or no perceptible sweetness. These are separate ideas.

A wine can be dry and tannic, dry and low in tannin, sweet and tannic, or sweet and low in tannin.

### Tannin versus acidity

Acidity usually feels fresh, tart or mouth-watering. Tannin feels more like grip and drying texture. A wine can have both noticeable acidity and noticeable tannin; one is not the opposite of the other.

### Tannin versus alcohol and body

Alcohol may feel warm or hot. Body describes the wine’s overall weight and fullness in the mouth. Tannin can contribute to structure and substance, but it is not body itself.

A light- or medium-bodied wine can still have noticeable tannin, while a full-bodied wine can have soft tannin.

## What do tannins feel like in Australian wines?

Variety is a useful clue, not a guarantee.

Australian **Shiraz**—the common Australian label term for Syrah—can range from supple and medium-bodied to concentrated and firmly structured. **Cabernet Sauvignon** often provides a clear example of a wine with noticeable tannin and structure, but Australian Cabernet varies with region, vintage, ripeness and winemaking.

**Pinot Noir** is often less tannic in impression than Cabernet Sauvignon, but it can still have clearly perceptible tannin. Skin contact, stem inclusion, ripeness, extraction and oak all influence the result.

A grape variety or regional name cannot tell you everything about the tannin in an individual bottle. The wine’s vintage, growing conditions, winemaking and maturation also matter.

## Do tannins soften with age?

Maturation can change the way tannin feels. Some wines become less aggressively astringent or seem more integrated with time, as tannins and other components undergo chemical changes.

However, tannins do not simply vanish, and ageing does not guarantee that every tannic wine will become softer or better. Tannin is one factor that can contribute to structure and ageing potential, alongside acidity, alcohol, fruit concentration, balance and storage conditions.

More tannin is not automatically a sign of higher quality.

## A simple way to taste tannin

You can try this with a small sip of red wine:

1. Notice whether the wine is sweet or dry.
2. Pay attention to its acidity: does it feel fresh or mouth-watering?
3. Let the wine move naturally around your mouth.
4. Focus on your gums and inner cheeks.
5. Ask whether the wine feels smooth or drying, soft or gripping, silky or rough.
6. Separate that sensation from alcohol warmth and bitterness.
7. Compare the feeling with strong black tea if a reference helps.

You do not need to assign the wine a precise tannin level. The aim is simply to recognise the sensation.

## Choosing a softer or more structured wine

Words such as **soft**, **supple** and **silky** often suggest a less aggressive tannin sensation. Words such as **firm**, **structured**, **grippy** and **chewy** suggest more noticeable tannin.

These descriptions are useful guides, not exact measurements. If you prefer less drying texture, ask a retailer or cellar-door host for a softer or more supple style. If you enjoy firmness and grip, ask for something more structured.

For a refresher on tasting wine, see [How to taste wine](/how-to-taste-wine/). You can also explore examples through [Shiraz](/what-is-shiraz/), [Pinot Noir](/what-is-pinot-noir/) and [Cabernet Sauvignon](/what-is-cabernet-sauvignon/).

## Tannin FAQs

### Are tannins only found in red wine?

No. Red wines usually show more noticeable tannin, but white and rosé wines can contain tannin from grape solids, skin contact, seed contact, oak or other winemaking choices.

### Are tannins bitter?

Tannin can contribute bitterness, but its main beginner-facing sensation is usually astringency: drying, gripping or puckering mouthfeel.

### How can I tell if a wine has tannin?

Notice whether the wine makes your gums and cheeks feel dry, rough or grippy after the sip. Strong black tea offers a useful sensory comparison.

### Which Australian wines have the most tannin?

There is no reliable universal ranking. Australian Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon can show noticeable tannin, while Pinot Noir can also be tannic depending on the wine’s region, ripeness and winemaking.

### Does more tannin mean better wine?

No. Tannin is a style and structural characteristic, not a score for quality. A wine can be enjoyable with firm tannin, soft tannin or very little noticeable tannin.
